additions.title: Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers' awareness?
additions.publisher: Brooke N. Macnamara and others, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (Springer, open access)
additions.quote: we discuss how artificial intelligence assistants might accelerate skill decay among experts and hinder skill acquisition among learners
additions.why: Peer-reviewed review by cognitive scientists setting out why AI assistance may speed the loss of expert skill, slow learners' acquisition of it, and hide both effects from the people concerned. That last point is why capability has to be tested and not assumed. Limits: the authors call it a 'theoretical perspective': it reasons from research on skill and automation and reports no new experiment; it says little research has yet measured the effect directly.

additions.title: AI-induced Deskilling in Medicine: A Mixed-Method Review and Research Agenda for Healthcare and Beyond
additions.publisher: Chiara Natali, Luca Marconi, Leslye Denisse Dias Duran and Federico Cabitza, Artificial Intelligence Review (Springer, open access)
additions.locator: Abstract; section 2.1 for the systematic review method
additions.quote: the erosion of medical expertise and the reduction of opportunities for skill acquisition due to AI-driven decision support systems
additions.why: Peer-reviewed review (2025) of the evidence on loss of clinical skill from AI decision support. It separates two harms the criterion covers, experienced staff losing skill and juniors never gaining it, maps them to the competencies tested in the UK physicians' clinical examination, and calls for monitoring and long-run studies. Limits: medicine only; the systematic part rests on a small number of studies; the authors call for longitudinal studies and real-time monitoring, which do not yet exist at scale.

additions.title: The Vicious Circles of Skill Erosion: A Case Study of Cognitive Automation
additions.publisher: Tapani Rinta-Kahila and others, Journal of the Association for Information Systems, 24(5), 1378-1412 (AIS eLibrary)
additions.locator: Abstract on the journal's own page
additions.quote: Such skill erosion may remain obscure, acknowledged by neither workers nor managers.
additions.why: The closest thing found to a study of the 'deskilling unnoticed' level in an ordinary business: an accounting firm whose staff lost expertise over several years of relying on software automation, which, the authors say, can go unacknowledged by workers and managers alike. They show how reliance breeds complacency in individuals and the organisation and weakens upkeep of competence. Limits: one firm; a case study in a peer-reviewed journal; software automation, not generative AI; only the abstract on the journal's page was read, not the full article.

additions.title: Enhanced FAA Oversight Could Reduce Hazards Associated With Increased Use of Flight Deck Automation (Audit Report AV-2016-013)
additions.publisher: U.S. Department of Transportation, Office of Inspector General
additions.quote: to use and monitor automation systems while also maintaining proficiency in manual flight operations
additions.why: An official audit finding that follows the two aviation sources already on the list: three years after the regulator's safety alert, the auditor found it could not tell how often pilots flew manually or whether airlines had acted. The lesson for a board is that advising people to keep skills up is not the same as checking that they do. Limits: United States; aviation; 2016; the report records the regulator's response, which was not followed up in this pass.

additions.title: FCA Handbook, Training and Competence sourcebook, TC 2.1: Assessing and maintaining competence
additions.quote: A firm must review on a regular and frequent basis employees' competence and take appropriate action to ensure that they remain competent for their role.
additions.why: A binding UK rule that requires what this criterion asks: regular review of whether people are still competent, and action if they are not, with guidance that this covers technical knowledge, skills and expertise. It is the model for 'capability retention monitored'. Limits: financial services only, and only the retail activities the sourcebook lists; it does not mention AI or automation; the page says the section was last updated on 6 April 2026 and the rule itself is dated 21 March 2016.

additions.title: GRI 404: Training and Education 2016
additions.quote: This disclosure helps demonstrate how an organization works to monitor and maintain the skill sets of its employees.
additions.why: The reporting standard under which an organisation would show the outside world that it keeps capability up: training hours per employee, programmes for upgrading skills, and the share of employees receiving regular performance and development reviews. It gives the 'monitored' and 'assured' levels a recognised form. Limits: voluntary; dated 2016; it measures training effort and reviews, not whether skills displaced by automation have been retained; it does not mention AI.

additions.title: OECD AI Principles, Principle 2.4: Building human capacity and preparing for labour market transformation
additions.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD.AI)
additions.locator: Rationale for this principle, third paragraph
additions.quote: skills development policies will need to focus on the distinctly human aspects necessary to complement AI systems, such as judgment, creative and critical thinking
additions.why: International comparator. The intergovernmental AI standard names the capabilities that have to be kept as AI spreads: judgement, creative and critical thinking and interpersonal communication. It gives a board a starting list for 'what stays human'. Limits: addressed to governments, not firms; non-binding; about skills policy in general and silent on skill decay from use of AI; the page carries no date (the OECD's principles page says they were adopted in 2019 and updated in May 2024).

additions.title: Managing technology that manages people: November 2025. A Social Partnership approach to algorithmic management systems in the Welsh public sector
additions.publisher: Welsh Government (guidance agreed by the Workforce Partnership Council)
additions.locator: Section 'Due diligence and consultation during buying or building systems'; general principle 4 (Building capability)
additions.quote: broader risks like work intensification, loss of expertise and overriding human judgment
additions.why: UK government guidance that names loss of expertise as a risk to be assessed before a workplace AI system is bought or built, alongside a standing commitment to build capability at every level of the workforce. It is the only UK official text found that treats deskilling as something to assess in advance. Limits: devolved public sector in Wales only; guidance, not law; covers systems used to manage workers; it does not say how the risk should be measured.

rejected.title: Gerlich, AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking (Societies, 2025)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 from the publisher. Not read. It would have supplied a UK sample.

rejected.title: General Medical Council, Skills fade: a review of the evidence that clinical and professional skills fade during time out of practice
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 on both the page and the PDF address tried. Not read. It would have supplied a UK rate of skill fade, which is still unverified.

rejected.title: Prudential Regulation Authority, Supervisory Statement SS2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management
rejected.reason: Read. Paragraph 4.6 ('Firms should avoid becoming empty shells') concerns the threshold conditions and organisational structure, not retention of staff skills; using it here would stretch it. Not added.

rejected.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 5.1.1R (competent employees rule)
rejected.reason: Read (the Handbook now serves rule text; the first pass got a script-only page). The rule is about employing competent people, and is already proposed for another criterion in this domain; TC 2.1.12R on maintaining competence is the better fit here.

rejected.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0, MAP 3.4 (operator and practitioner proficiency)
rejected.reason: Read. About proficiency with the AI system, not retention of the underlying human skill, and the same passage is already proposed for another criterion in this domain. Not added.

rejected.title: Lehmann, Cornelius and Sting, AI Meets the Classroom: When Do Large Language Models Harm Learning? (arXiv 2409.09047)
rejected.reason: Abstract read: two laboratory experiments with students found 'no effect of LLMs on overall learning outcomes'. Student learning, not workplace skill; noted as mixed evidence but not added.

rejected.title: Office of Rail and Road, Developing and maintaining staff competence (Railway Safety Publication 1)
rejected.reason: HTTP 404 at the address tried; no other address found in this pass. Not read.

rejected.title: BEA final report on Air France flight 447
rejected.reason: HTTP 404 at the address tried. Not read.

brief_check: One nuance, not a contradiction. The brief says UK duties on capability 'concern health and safety'; the FCA's Training and Competence rule TC 2.1.12R is a binding duty outside health and safety to review employees' competence regularly and keep them competent, though only for listed retail financial activities and with no mention of AI. 'No UK law addresses loss of skill through AI' still stands. Evidence remains mixed and thin: the two peer-reviewed reviews say direct measurement is scarce, and one student experiment read found no overall learning effect.
